kurals.tamil:
சுழன்றும்ஏர்ப் பின்னது உலகம் அதனால்
உழந்தும் உழவே தலை.
kurals.transliteration:
Suzhandrum-Erp pinnadhu ulagam adhanaal
uzhandhum uzhavae thalai.
kurals.meaning: However the world wanders from one trade to another, it still ends up following the plough; so, for all its hardship, farming is the foremost of occupations.
kurals.elementary: People can be bakers, builders, drivers or doctors, but every one of them still needs lunch, and lunch starts in a farmer's field. Farming is hard, sweaty work, yet Valluvar says it is the most important job of all, because every other job leans on it.
kurals.university: The chapter opens with its thesis: suzhandrum (சுழன்றும், 'though it whirls about', i.e. though people turn to many other callings) the world is Erp pinnadhu (ஏர்ப் பின்னது, 'behind the plough'), so uzhandhum (உழந்தும், 'even though it means toil') uzhavu is thalai (தலை, 'head, chief'). Puliyur Kesikan, in the commentarial line of Parimelazhagar, reads suzhandrum as people roaming through other trades because they see the hardship of farming, and the second line as a concession: farming is best despite that hardship; Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar agree. Uzhavu (ch. 104) stands in the Kudiyiyal section of Porutpal, between Kudiseyalvagai (ch. 103) and Nalkuravu (ch. 105, poverty), so Valluvar presents productive labour as the household's answer to want. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “All living bodies subsist on food grains, which are produced from rains.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna places food grain at the base of the whole chain of life, ritual and duty.
hinduism.tie_back: If every body lives on grain, the world really does stand behind whoever grows it.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.14 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda, vedabase.io)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; it shows that all life depends on grain but credits rain and sacrifice rather than the ploughman's labour.

christianity.quote_or_event: “cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life; … In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground”
christianity.explanation: After the fall, Adam is told that human bread will come only from hard toil on the soil.
christianity.tie_back: Genesis, like the Kural, makes painful tillage the condition every human life rests on.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (ellipsis marks omitted words); it shares the theme of toilsome but necessary tillage, framed as a curse rather than praise.

islam.quote_or_event: “And have you seen that [seed] which you sow? Is it you who makes it grow, or are We the grower?”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an points to sowing as a sign that all human sustenance depends on growth people do not control.
islam.tie_back: Both texts treat sowing and harvest as what all human life hangs on, though the Qur'an credits God where the Kural praises the farmer.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud; it shares the dependence-on-agriculture theme but its point is God's agency, not the farmer's primacy.

judaism.quote_or_event: “All craftsmen are destined to stand upon and work the land”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar reads Ezekiel 27:29 to mean that every craftsman will end up working the land.
judaism.tie_back: This comes close to the Kural's picture of a world that wanders through trades and still ends up behind the plough.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 63a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria (bold-face markup removed); in the same passage Rabbi Elazar also calls farming the lowliest work and other sages prefer trade, so the Talmud is more divided than the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “by whatsoever activity a householder earns his living, whether by farming, by trading, by rearing cattle, by archery, by service under the king, or by any other kind of craft — at that he becomes skillful and is not lazy.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists farming first among the livelihoods in which a householder must be skilled and tireless.
buddhism.tie_back: Farming heads the Buddha's list, much as the Kural ranks it first, though he does not argue that it is supreme.
buddhism.source: Dighajanu (Vyagghapajja) Sutta, AN 8.54 (tr. Narada Thera, accesstoinsight.org)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; farming is listed first, but the sutta values diligence in any trade rather than ranking agriculture above the others.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain tradition holds that the first Tirthankara, Rishabhanatha, taught people the means of livelihood at the start of the present age, before he renounced the world; later Jain writers name these as asi (arms), masi (writing) and krishi (agriculture).
jainism.explanation: In the Jain account, settled human life begins when Rishabha teaches cultivation, among other arts, to a humanity that can no longer live from wish-fulfilling trees.
jainism.tie_back: In this account agriculture is one of the founding arts of civilised life, which fits the Kural's claim that all society trails behind the plough.
jainism.source: Life of Rishabha, Kalpa Sūtra (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22) and later Digambara purāṇa tradition (asi-masi-kṛṣi)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase only: the Kalpa Sutra page could not be fetched this session and the asi-masi-krishi triad is from later tradition; Jain ethics also counts ploughing as harmful to earth-bodies, so the fit is partial.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For the gods keep hidden from men the means of life. Else you would easily do work enough in a day to supply you for a full year even without working”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod explains, through the Prometheus myth, why people must labour on the land for their bread.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod also makes hard farm work an unavoidable law of human life.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 42-46 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White, 1914, sacred-texts.com)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it supports the 'toil is unavoidable' half of the Kural more than the 'farming is supreme' half.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It was an excellent saying of his who named husbandry ‘the mother and nurse of all the arts,’ … where the land is forced to remain desert, the spring that feeds the other arts is dried up”
philosophy.explanation: Xenophon's Socrates calls agriculture the source that keeps every other art alive.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural's claim that all trades follow the plough.
philosophy.source: Xenophon, Oeconomicus 5.17 (tr. H.G. Dakyns, Project Gutenberg)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (ellipsis marks omitted words); a near one-to-one statement that agriculture comes first.

kurals.tamil:
உழுவார் உலகத்தார்க்கு ஆணிஅஃ தாற்றாது
எழுவாரை எல்லாம் பொறுத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Uzhuvaar ulagaththaarkku aaNi-aq thaatraadhu
ezhuvaarai ellaam poRuththu.
kurals.meaning: Those who plough are the linchpin of the world, because they carry everyone who cannot till the soil and turns to other work.
kurals.elementary: A wagon wheel has a small pin that holds it on the axle. Without that pin the wheel falls off and the whole cart stops. Valluvar says farmers are that pin: they feed everyone else, so the whole world keeps rolling because of them.
kurals.university: The image is the aaNi (ஆணி), the linchpin or axle-pin that keeps a cart's wheel in place; the ploughmen are the aaNi of ulagaththaar (உலகத்தார், 'the people of the world'). The second line gives the reason: aqthu aatraadhu ezhuvaarai ellaam poRuththu (அஃது ஆற்றாது எழுவாரை எல்லாம் பொறுத்து), 'bearing all who, unable to do that (ploughing), go off to other work'. Puliyur Kesikan, in the line of Parimelazhagar, glosses ezhuvaar as those who leave farming for other trades and are still fed by the farmers' grain; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it the same way, and Pope gives 'linch-pin of the world'. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; ytamizh hyphenates the transliteration aaNi-aq.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The ploughshare ploughing makes the food that feeds us, and with its feet cuts through the path it follows.”
hinduism.explanation: In a hymn on liberality, the Vedic poet names the plough as the maker of the food everyone eats.
hinduism.tie_back: The Rig Veda and the Kural both say that the plough feeds us all.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.7 (tr. Ralph T.H. Griffith, 1896, sacred-texts.com)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near-direct parallel to the farmer as the world's provider.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Moreover the profit of the earth is for all: the king himself is served by the field.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher observes that the yield of the land supports everyone, the king included.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's linchpin, the field carries everyone, from commoner to king.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong thematic match, though it speaks of the field rather than of the farmer.

islam.quote_or_event: “There is none amongst the Muslims who plants a tree or sows seeds, and then a bird, or a person or an animal eats from it, but is regarded as a charitable gift for him.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet counts every mouthful taken from a crop, even by birds and animals, as the sower's charity.
islam.tie_back: The farmer feeds all who do not sow, which is the Kural's picture of the ploughman bearing the world.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; it closely matches the idea of the farmer sustaining others.

judaism.quote_or_event: “You make the grass grow for the cattle, and herbage for humans’ labor that they may get food out of the earth— … and bread that sustains human life.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist praises the order in which human labour on the earth yields the bread that keeps people alive.
judaism.tie_back: Bread from tilled earth sustains human life, which is the support the Kural credits to farmers.
judaism.source: Psalms 104:14-15 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (ellipsis marks omitted words); a reasonable fit, though the psalm praises God's provision more than the farmer.

buddhism.quote_or_event: At sowing time the brahman Kasi Bharadvaja had about 500 ploughs yoked and was running a food distribution when the Buddha arrived for alms; he told the Buddha that he ploughed and sowed before he ate, and that a contemplative should do the same.
buddhism.explanation: The scene shows a farming household whose harvest feeds many people, including wandering monks who come for alms.
buddhism.tie_back: The farmer's food distribution feeding the non-ploughing alms-seeker is the Kural's ploughman carrying 'all who cannot till.'
buddhism.source: Kasi Bharadvaja Sutta, Sn 1.4 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu, accesstoinsight.org)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from the verified opening of the sutta; the Buddha goes on to reject the claim that the farmer is superior, so this is only a partial fit.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Dasavaikalika Sutra opens by comparing the true monk to a bee that drinks a little from many flowers without harming them, gathering alms from householders' kitchens without burdening any one of them.
jainism.explanation: Jain mendicants do not cook or farm. They live on small portions of food that householders have prepared for themselves.
jainism.tie_back: This is a Jain picture of the non-producing world being carried by householders' food, the dependence the Kural describes.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified against a live text this session; the simile is about harmless alms-taking, and Jainism does not praise farmers as such.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Both gods and men are angry with a man who lives idle, for in nature he is like the stingless drones who waste the labour of the bees, eating without working”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod compares people who eat without working to drones living on the bees' labour.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's linchpin seen from the other side: workers carry those who do not till.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 303-306 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White, 1914, sacred-texts.com)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; Hesiod condemns the idle, while the Kural only notes that the farmer supports non-farmers, so the fit is partial.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Cultivators of the earth are the most valuable citizens. They are the most vigorous, the most independant, the most virtuous, and they are tied to their country and wedded to it’s liberty and interests by the most lasting bands.”
philosophy.explanation: Jefferson ranks farmers above every other class as the foundation of the republic.
philosophy.tie_back: Jefferson's 'most valuable citizens' are the Kural's linchpin of the world, put in civic terms.
philosophy.source: Thomas Jefferson to John Jay, 23 August 1785 (Founders Online, National Archives)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim, including Jefferson's spellings; a strong thematic match, though his argument is political rather than about feeding others.

kurals.tamil:
உழுதுண்டு வாழ்வாரே வாழ்வார்மற் றெல்லாம்
தொழுதுண்டு பின்செல் பவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
UzhudhuNdu vaazhvaarae vaazhvaarmaR Rellaam
thozhudhuNdu pinsel pavar.
kurals.meaning: Only those who live by ploughing and eating its yield truly live; everyone else eats by bowing to others and walks behind them.
kurals.elementary: Imagine growing your own tomatoes and eating them, compared with always having to ask someone else to share. Valluvar says the farmer who grows his own food can stand tall, while people who must keep asking others for food have to follow behind them.
kurals.university: The couplet sets uzhudhu uNdu (உழுது உண்டு, 'ploughing, eating') against thozhudhu uNdu (தொழுது உண்டு, 'bowing, eating'), a deliberate rhyme in which a single consonant separates self-reliance from servility. Puliyur Kesikan, following Parimelazhagar, glosses those who plough as urimai vaazhvinar (உரிமை வாழ்வினர், 'those who live by right'), and says the rest eat by paying court to others and pinsel (பின்செல், 'follow behind') them; Solomon Pappaiah adds that the farmer ploughs for others as well as for himself. The ideal is economic independence rather than caste or rank. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Play not with dice: no, cultivate thy corn-land. Enjoy the gain, and deem that wealth sufficient.”
hinduism.explanation: At the end of the gambler's lament, the poet tells him to give up dice and live honourably from his own field.
hinduism.tie_back: Living from one's own tilled land, instead of a ruinous dependence, is the life the Kural calls true living.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.34.13 (tr. Ralph T.H. Griffith, 1896, sacred-texts.com)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong fit for self-reliant farming, though the contrast is with gambling, not with servility.

christianity.quote_or_event: “and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you; That ye may walk honestly toward them that are without, and that ye may have lack of nothing.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to support themselves by manual work so that they owe nothing to anyone.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Paul ties self-supporting labour to an independent and dignified life.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong match on independence through one's own labour, though it is not specifically about farming.

islam.quote_or_event: “Nobody has ever eaten a better meal than that which one has earned by working with one's own hands. The Prophet of Allah, David used to eat from the earnings of his manual labor.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet ranks food earned by one's own hands above every other kind.
islam.tie_back: This is close to the Kural's uzhudhuNdu: the best life eats what its own hands have earned.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com (the ﷺ honorific omitted); a near one-to-one match, though it covers all manual labour, not only farming.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He who tills his land shall have food in plenty, But one who pursues vanities is devoid of sense.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs contrasts the steady plenty of the person who works his own land with the folly of chasing empty things.
judaism.tie_back: Proverbs and the Kural both set the self-sufficient tiller against those who live otherwise.
judaism.source: Proverbs 12:11 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a strong thematic fit, though the foil is vanity rather than dependence.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is the case where the son of a good family has wealth earned through his efforts & enterprise, amassed through the strength of his arm, and piled up through the sweat of his brow, righteous wealth righteously gained … This is called the bliss of having.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names the joy of self-earned wealth, together with the joy of owing nothing to anyone, among a householder's legitimate happinesses.
buddhism.tie_back: The 'bliss of having' and of debtlessness is the independent life the Kural reserves for those who eat by their own ploughing.
buddhism.source: Anana Sutta, AN 4.62 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu, accesstoinsight.org)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (ellipsis marks omitted words); strong on self-earned independence, but not specific to farming and ranked below blamelessness.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain householder ethics, as set out by Hemacandra, lists fifteen forbidden trades (karmādāna) for lay followers; one is sphoṭa-karma, earning a living by breaking up the earth through digging or ploughing, because it destroys countless earth- and soil-dwelling beings.
jainism.explanation: Jainism praises honest, self-supporting livelihood but steers lay followers away from trades that do heavy violence to living beings, and tilling the soil is among them.
jainism.tie_back: Here Jain teaching diverges from the Kural: it values self-reliance but does not hold up ploughing as the noblest way to earn it.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra 3 (the fifteen karmādānas), as summarised in Jain ethical literature
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified against a live text this session; included as an honest contrast, because Jain ethics conflicts with the Kural's praise of ploughing.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “work, high-born Perses, that Hunger may hate you, and venerable Demeter richly crowned may love you and fill your barn with food; for Hunger is altogether a meet comrade for the sluggard.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells his brother that only steady farm work wins Demeter's favour and a full barn.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod's full barn, earned by one's own farming, is the self-reliant life the Kural praises.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 299-302 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White, 1914, sacred-texts.com)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a good fit for self-supporting farming, though the dependence-versus-independence contrast is only implied.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But of all the occupations by which gain is secured, none is better than agriculture, none more profitable, none more delightful, none more becoming to a freeman.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero ranks farming above every other way of earning a living, as the one most fitting for a free person.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero's 'becoming to a freeman' answers the Kural's contrast between the farmer and those who must bow to others.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis 1.151 (tr. Walter Miller, Loeb 1913, LacusCurtius)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius; a near match on farming as the free and noblest livelihood.

kurals.tamil:
பலகுடை நீழலும் தங்குடைக்கீழ்க் காண்பர்
அலகுடை நீழ லவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Palakudai neezhalum thangutaikkeezhk kaaNpar
alakutai neezha lavar.
kurals.meaning: Farmers whose wealth is the shade of ripening grain will see the shade of many kings' umbrellas gathered under their own king's umbrella.
kurals.elementary: In old Tamil kingdoms a king's royal umbrella stood for his rule. Valluvar says that a land with plenty of grain becomes so strong and attractive that other lands come under its protection. Good farms make a strong country.
kurals.university: The couplet plays on kudai (குடை, the royal parasol, emblem of sovereignty) and neezhal (நீழல், 'shade'). alakudai neezhalavar (அலகுடை நீழலவர்) are those who have the shade of alaku (அலகு, ears of grain), that is, prosperous farmers; Puliyur Kesikan, following Parimelazhagar, glosses them as nel udaiyavar, 'owners of paddy', and also as karunaiyaalar, 'the compassionate', taking neezhal as the cool shade of grace (thannali), a reading Mu. Varadarasanar keeps. Such farmers 'see' the umbrellas of many kings come under their own king's umbrella, because grain surplus makes a realm strong. Solomon Pappaiah takes a softer line: people of other lands come to desire the farmers' ruler. Pope's 'Whose fields are shaded by the waving grain' brings out the pun. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; only word spacing differs.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “They therefore constructed places of refuge … and formed villages and cities … Having thus provided security against the weather, men next began to employ themselves in manual labour, as a means of livelihood, (and cultivated) the seventeen kinds of useful grain”
hinduism.explanation: The Vishnu Purana describes organised settlements and grain cultivation arising together as the basis of ordered human society.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts make grain-growing the foundation of a secure, ordered polity, though the Purana does not speak of one kingdom drawing in others.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (ellipses mark omitted words); it links agriculture with settled polity but lacks the Kural's point about the farmer's strength extending the king's rule.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And all countries came into Egypt to Joseph for to buy corn; because that the famine was so sore in all lands.”
christianity.explanation: Because Egypt stored grain in the years of plenty, every land had to turn to Pharaoh's Egypt in the famine.
christianity.tie_back: A land rich in grain draws other nations under its influence, which is the Kural's 'many umbrellas under one'.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong narrative parallel for grain giving a realm power over other lands.

islam.quote_or_event: “There was for [the tribe of] Saba' in their dwelling place a sign: two [fields of] gardens on the right and on the left. [They were told], ‘Eat from the provisions of your Lord and be grateful to Him. A good land [have you], and a forgiving Lord.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an recalls the kingdom of Sheba, made prosperous by the gardens on either side of its land.
islam.tie_back: Sheba shows the Kural's link between abundant fields and a flourishing realm.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud; it links farmland to a kingdom's prosperity but says nothing about extending rule over others, and the story ends in Sheba's ingratitude.

judaism.quote_or_event: “All the days of Solomon, Judah and Israel from Dan to Beer-sheba dwelt in safety, every family under its own vine and fig tree.”
judaism.explanation: Solomon's reign is remembered for secure, settled farm life spread across the whole land.
judaism.tie_back: Every family under its own vine within one secure kingdom echoes the Kural's shade of grain and shade of the king's umbrella.
judaism.source: 1 Kings 5:5 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition 2023, via Sefaria; 4:25 in Christian numbering)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; it pairs agricultural plenty with a strong kingdom but lacks the idea of drawing in other realms.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kutadanta Sutta, a king facing banditry is advised to give food and seed-corn to those who farm and keep cattle, capital to traders, and wages to officials. Once the people are prosperous and content, the realm becomes peaceful, so that people can live with open doors.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha retells this advice to show that a realm made prosperous through its farmers is stronger than one held down by force.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the farmers' prosperity becomes the strength of the king's rule.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the live page could not be loaded this session. A reasonable match on farm prosperity as the base of royal power, without the idea of expanding over other kingdoms.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jain universal history tells how Bharata, Rishabhanatha's eldest son, became the first cakravartin of this age and brought all six divisions of Bharatavarsha under one rule; the same tradition credits his father with teaching the arts of cultivation.
jainism.explanation: In the Jain account, a realm built on the arts Rishabha taught, farming among them, grows into a universal kingdom under Bharata.
jainism.tie_back: Many umbrellas under one, the Kural's image, matches Bharata's unification, though the Jain story does not credit the farmers for it.
jainism.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 1 (tr. Helen M. Johnson)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified against a live text this session; Jain sources treat Bharata's conquest ambivalently and do not tie it to agriculture, so this is a weak next-best match.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Demeter entrusts the Eleusinian prince Triptolemus with wheat and a chariot drawn by winged dragons, and he flies over the inhabited earth sowing it.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the myth, the gift of grain spreads outward from one small kingdom to all lands.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Grain from one realm reaches every land, a mythic version of the Kural's farmer whose king's shade covers many others.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the live text was not re-checked this session. The myth is about spreading agriculture, not political dominion, so the fit is partial.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “it is from the farming class that the bravest men and the sturdiest soldiers come, their calling is most highly respected, their livelihood is most assured and is looked on with the least hostility”
philosophy.explanation: Cato argues that a farming population gives the state its strongest soldiers and its most loyal citizens.
philosophy.tie_back: For Cato, as for the Kural, a strong farming base is what lets a ruler's power stand and spread.
philosophy.source: Cato the Elder, De Agricultura, Preface 4 (tr. W.D. Hooper and H.B. Ash, Loeb 1934, LacusCurtius)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius; strong on farmers as the strength of the state, though it does not speak of absorbing other realms.

kurals.tamil:
இரவார் இரப்பார்க்கொன்று ஈவர் கரவாது
கைசெய்தூண் மாலை யவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Iravaar irappaarkkondru eevar karavaadhu
kaiseydhooN maalai yavar.
kurals.meaning: Those whose way of life is to eat by the work of their own hands never beg, and they give to those who beg without hiding what they have.
kurals.elementary: A girl who grows her own strawberries never has to ask anyone for strawberries. And when a friend asks for some, she shares happily instead of hiding the basket. Working with your own hands lets you be both proud and generous.
kurals.university: kai seydhu ooN maalaiyavar (கைசெய்து ஊண் மாலையவர்) means 'those whose nature (maalai, மாலை) is to eat by the work of their hands'. Puliyur Kesikan, following Parimelazhagar, identifies them with farmers (uzhavar) whose effort yields food. Two consequences follow: iravaar (இரவார், 'they do not beg') and they give irappaarkku ondru (இரப்பார்க்கு ஒன்று, 'something to those who beg') karavaadhu (கரவாது, 'without concealment'). Mu. Varadarasanar widens the subject to all who labour with their hands (thozhilaalar), while Solomon Pappaiah and Kesikan keep the focus on ploughing. The couplet also looks ahead to the later chapters Iravu (106) and Iravachcham (107) on begging. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Bounteous is he who gives unto the beggar who comes to him in want of food and feeble.”
hinduism.explanation: The hymn praises the man with food who freely gives to a hungry petitioner.
hinduism.tie_back: The hymn's bounteous giver is the Kural's self-supporting farmer who gives to askers without concealment.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 10.117.3 (tr. Ralph T.H. Griffith, 1896, sacred-texts.com)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong on giving to askers, and the same hymn (v. 7) praises the plough, but this verse does not mention self-support.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the converted thief to support himself by honest handwork so that he will have something to give to the needy.
christianity.tie_back: Working with one's own hands in order to give to those in need is almost exactly the Kural's teaching.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match on labouring with one's own hands so as to give.

islam.quote_or_event: “It is better for anyone of you to take a rope (and cut) and bring a bundle of wood (from the forest) over his back and sell it and Allah will save his face (from the Hell-Fire) because of that, rather than to ask the people who may give him or not.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet prefers the humblest manual labour to begging from others.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's iravaar, 'they do not beg', grounded in work with one's own hands.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; strong on not begging through manual work, though it does not cover the giving half of the Kural.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not reap all the way to the edges of your field, or gather the gleanings of your harvest. … you shall leave them for the poor and the stranger”
judaism.explanation: The Torah requires every farmer to leave part of the harvest for the poor and the stranger.
judaism.tie_back: The farmer's own harvest becomes open, unconcealed giving, the generosity the Kural expects of those who eat by their own work.
judaism.source: Leviticus 19:9-10 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (ellipsis marks omitted words); strong on the farmer's duty to give, though it says nothing about not begging.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “using the wealth earned through his efforts & enterprise, amassed through the strength of his arm, and piled up through the sweat of his brow, righteous wealth righteously gained — provides his friends & associates with pleasure & satisfaction”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the benefits of self-earned wealth: supporting oneself, one's family and friends, and giving offerings to contemplatives.
buddhism.tie_back: Wealth 'amassed through the strength of his arm' and shared with others is the Kural's kai seydhu ooN joined to generous giving.
buddhism.source: Adiya Sutta, AN 5.41 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu, accesstoinsight.org)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong on giving from wealth earned by one's own work, though it is not specific to farming or to beggars.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The husbandmen throw the corn on high ground and on low ground, hoping (for a return). For the like motive give unto me; I may be the field which may produce merit (as the return for your benevolence).”
jainism.explanation: The Jain monk Harikesa, begging at a sacrifice, asks the priests to give as freely as farmers sow, since a gift to the worthy yields merit as seed yields grain.
jainism.tie_back: The farmer who sows without stinting is the model for generous giving to an asker, which is the Kural's second line.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, sacred-texts.com)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it uses the farmer as the image of liberal giving, but the speaker is the asker and the topic is merit, not self-support.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Else, afterwards, you may chance to be in want, and go begging to other men's houses, but without avail; as you have already come to me. But I will give you no more nor give you further measure.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns his idle brother Perses that whoever neglects the seasons of farm work ends up begging from door to door.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod gives the negative of the Kural's lesson: whoever does not work the land with his own hands will have to beg.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 394-397 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White, 1914, sacred-texts.com)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong on farming versus begging, but Hesiod is refusing to give, which is the opposite of the Kural's generous farmer.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Earth, in the first place, freely offers to those that labour all things necessary to the life of man … She is the generous hostess; she keeps open house for the stranger.”
philosophy.explanation: Xenophon's Socrates praises farming because the land rewards labour and makes hospitality to strangers possible.
philosophy.tie_back: The farmer's 'open house for the stranger' is the Kural's ungrudging gift to the asker, made possible by labour on the land.
philosophy.source: Xenophon, Oeconomicus ch. 5 (tr. H.G. Dakyns, Project Gutenberg)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (ellipsis marks omitted words); it praises the generosity that farming makes possible, but credits the earth rather than the farmer's character.

kurals.tamil:
உழவினார் கைம்மடங்கின் இல்லை விழைவதூஉம்
விட்டேம்என் பார்க்கும் நிலை.
kurals.transliteration:
Uzhavinaar kaimmadangin illai vizhaivadhooum
vittaemen paarkkum nilai.
kurals.meaning: If the farmers fold their hands, even those who say 'we have given up everything we desired' cannot keep to their way of life.
kurals.elementary: Even people who have given up toys, money and fancy things to live a simple, holy life still need a bowl of rice each day. If farmers stopped working, those holy people would go hungry too. So everyone, even a saint, depends on the farmer.
kurals.university: uzhavinaar kai madangin (உழவினார் கை மடங்கின்) means 'if the ploughmen's hands fold (stop working)'. Then illai ... nilai (இல்லை ... நிலை): there is no standing even for those who say vizhaivadhooum vittaem (விழைவதூஉம் விட்டேம், 'we have renounced even what is desired'), that is, the ascetics (thuRavigaL). Puliyur Kesikan, in Parimelazhagar's line, takes vizhaivadhu as the food everyone desires and reads nilai as the renunciant's steadiness in his dharma; Solomon Pappaiah agrees, and Kalaignar says even renouncers must look to the farmer's hand. The couplet links back to the Aram section's chapter on ascetics (Neeththaar Perumai, ch. 3) and to rain as the support of austerity (Kural 19), placing the household economy beneath the renunciant. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the alapedai lengthening -ooum is printed in both.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As all living creatures subsist by receiving support from air, even so (the members of) all orders subsist by receiving support from the householder.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu teaches that students, hermits and ascetics all live on the support of the householder, whose order is therefore the most excellent.
hinduism.tie_back: If the householder-farmer's hands stop, the renunciant orders fail, which is exactly the Kural's claim.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near match on renunciants depending on householders, though Manu does not single out the farmer.

christianity.quote_or_event: “he that ploweth should plow in hope; and that he that thresheth in hope should be partaker of his hope. If we have sown unto you spiritual things, is it a great thing if we shall reap your carnal things?”
christianity.explanation: Paul argues that those who serve spiritually may rightly be fed by the material harvest of those they serve.
christianity.tie_back: Spiritual workers live on others' ploughing and threshing, the dependence of renouncers on farmers that the Kural names.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong structural parallel, though Paul is defending the apostles' right to support rather than praising farmers.

islam.quote_or_event: “There were two brothers during the time of the Messenger of Allah (s.a.w). One of them used to come to the prophet (s.a.w), and the other had some business. The businessman among them complained to the Prophet (s.a.w) about his brother, so he said: ‘Perhaps you are provided for because of him.’”
islam.explanation: When the working brother complains about supporting his devout brother, the Prophet suggests that his provision may come for the sake of that devotion.
islam.tie_back: The hadith shows the same pairing of a worker supporting a devotee that the Kural describes, though it stresses the devotee's spiritual worth.
islam.source: Jami` at-Tirmidhi 2345 (sunnah.com; graded Sahih by Darussalam)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; the same relationship as the Kural, but the hadith reverses the emphasis by suggesting the worker depends spiritually on the devotee.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Where there is no bread, there is no Torah; where there is no Torah, there is no bread.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah teaches that sacred study cannot survive without material sustenance, and the reverse.
judaism.tie_back: Without bread, the life of study and holiness cannot stand, which is the Kural's point about renunciants and farmers.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 3:17 (tr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a near one-to-one match, though the mishnah also makes the dependence run both ways.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “I, contemplative, plow & sow. Having plowed & sown, I eat. You, too, contemplative, should plow & sow. Having plowed & sown, you (will) eat.”
buddhism.explanation: A brahman farmer challenges the Buddha, who has come for alms, to plough before he eats. The Buddha replies that his own 'ploughing' is faith, austerity and discernment, which bears the deathless as its fruit.
buddhism.tie_back: The sutta stages the Kural's question of how renunciants live off farmers, and the Buddha answers that they repay the farmer with a spiritual harvest.
buddhism.source: Kasi Bharadvaja Sutta, Sn 1.4 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu, accesstoinsight.org)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it addresses the same dependence directly, though it defends the monk where the Kural stresses the farmer's importance.

jainism.quote_or_event: “I am a chaste Sramana, controlling myself; I have no property, nothing belonging to me, and do not cook my food; I have come for food which is dressed for somebody else at the time when I call. … know that I subsist by begging; let the mendicant get what is left of the rest.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain monk Harikesa explains that a renunciant owns nothing and does not cook, and lives only on food that householders have prepared for themselves.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain mendicant depends entirely on householders' food, so if the farmers' hands folded, his discipline could not continue, as the Kural says.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.9-10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, sacred-texts.com)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (ellipsis marks omitted words); a strong match on renunciants depending on householders' food, though farming itself is not named.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “In the fields the oxen drew many a curved plough in vain, and much white barley was cast upon the land without avail. So she would have destroyed the whole race of man with cruel famine and have robbed them who dwell on Olympus of their glorious right of gifts and sacrifices”
greek_mythology.explanation: When grieving Demeter halts the harvest, humanity faces famine and even the gods lose the offerings they live by.
greek_mythology.tie_back: When the plough fails, even those above ordinary life lose their support, which is the Kural's point about renunciants.
greek_mythology.source: Homeric Hymn to Demeter 305-312 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White, sacred-texts.com)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a striking parallel of a higher order depending on the harvest, with gods in place of ascetics.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “such operations as the breaking up of fallow with the plough, the sowing of seed, the planting of trees, the pasturing and herding of flocks, are one and all open-air employments on which the supply of products necessary to life depends.”
philosophy.explanation: Xenophon's Ischomachus names ploughing and sowing as the outdoor work on which the whole household's necessities depend.
philosophy.tie_back: Every life, whatever its station, depends on the ploughing hand, and the Kural extends this even to renunciants.
philosophy.source: Xenophon, Oeconomicus ch. 7 (tr. H.G. Dakyns, Project Gutenberg)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it makes the general dependence point but does not mention ascetics or renunciants.

kurals.tamil:
தொடிப்புழுதி கஃசா உணக்கின் பிடித்தெருவும்
வேண்டாது சாலப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thotippuzhudhi kaqsaa uNakkin pitiththeruvum
vaeNtaadhu saalap padum.
kurals.meaning: If ploughed soil is dried until one measure of it shrinks to a quarter, the crop will grow abundantly without even a handful of manure.
kurals.elementary: If you dig a garden, break up the lumps and let the sun dry the soil really well, the plants grow strong even without extra fertiliser. Getting the ground ready carefully is half the work of farming.
kurals.university: This is one of the Kural's most technical couplets. thodi (தொடி) and kaqsu (கஃசு) are weights: one palam and a quarter palam. thodippuzhudhi kaqsaa uNakkin (தொடிப்புழுதி கஃசா உணக்கின்) means 'if you dry a palam of ploughed dust down to a quarter-palam', that is, plough repeatedly and sun-dry the soil until three-quarters of its moisture weight is lost. Then piditheruvum vaeNdaadhu (பிடித்து எருவும் வேண்டாது, 'not needing even a fistful of manure') the crop saalap padum (சாலப் படும், 'will flourish greatly'). Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar give this measure-based reading, following Parimelazhagar; Solomon Pappaiah converts it to about 35 grams reduced to 8.75 grams, and Kalaignar stresses repeated ploughing. Pope keeps the weights as 'ounce' and 'quarter-ounce'. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Happily let the shares turn up the plough-land, happily go the ploughers with the oxen.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic field-blessing hymn asks that the ploughshares turn the soil well so that the land will bear.
hinduism.tie_back: The Vedic poet, like Valluvar, treats a well-turned field as the foundation of a good harvest.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 4.57.8 (tr. Ralph T.H. Griffith, 1896, sacred-texts.com)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a blessing on ploughing rather than the Kural's technique of drying the soil, so only a general match.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But other fell into good ground, and brought forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the sower, only seed that falls on good, prepared ground gives a great harvest.
christianity.tie_back: The quality of the soil decides the yield, which is the Kural's point about well-worked earth needing no manure.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it shares the good-soil-equals-abundance idea, but the parable is spiritual and says nothing about how to prepare soil.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the good land - its vegetation emerges by permission of its Lord; but that which is bad - nothing emerges except sparsely, with difficulty.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an contrasts good land that yields readily with poor land that yields only grudgingly.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, well-conditioned soil gives freely while poor soil struggles.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud; it shares the soil-quality theme but has no ploughing or drying technique, and its main point is a parable about hearts.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Do those who plow to sow Plow all the time, Breaking up and furrowing their land? When they have smoothed its surface, Do they not rather broadcast black cumin … For they are taught the right manner, Their God instructs them.”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah describes the farmer's orderly sequence of breaking, furrowing and smoothing the soil before sowing, and calls it divinely taught skill.
judaism.tie_back: Isaiah and the Kural both describe careful soil preparation as the farmer's real expertise.
judaism.source: Isaiah 28:24-26 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (ellipsis marks omitted words); a good fit on preparing the soil, though without the drying measure or the point about manure.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is the case where a farming householder quickly gets his field well-plowed & well-harrowed. Having quickly gotten his field well-plowed & well-harrowed, he quickly plants the seed.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names thorough ploughing and harrowing as the first urgent duty of a farmer, then compares it to a monk's training.
buddhism.tie_back: Well-ploughed, well-harrowed ground before sowing is exactly the preparation the Kural praises.
buddhism.source: Accayika Sutta, AN 3.91 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu, accesstoinsight.org; AN 3.93 in other numbering)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong match on careful soil preparation, used here as a simile for spiritual training.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Acaranga Sutra teaches that the earth itself is inhabited by earth-bodied souls (prithvikaya jivas) and warns that those who dig and work the soil for their own ends injure countless such beings.
jainism.explanation: In Jain cosmology, soil is alive, so working and breaking it carries a moral cost that the monk must avoid entirely.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain view sharply contrasts with the Kural's practical advice to plough and dry the soil thoroughly, which from a Jain standpoint multiplies harm.
jainism.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.1.2 (on earth-bodies; tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not re-verified against a live text this session; included as an honest doctrinal contrast because no Jain text endorses intensive tillage.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Plough in the spring; but fallow broken up in the summer will not belie your hopes. Sow fallow land when the soil is still getting light: fallow land is a defender from harm and a soother of children.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod advises breaking up fallow in summer, so that the soil is dried and loosened before sowing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Summer-worked, sun-dried fallow giving a reliable crop closely matches the Kural's dried soil that needs no manure.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 462-464 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White, 1914, sacred-texts.com)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong technical parallel on working and drying the soil, though without the specific measure.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Would he not, when he was in earnest, follow the rules of husbandry, plant his seeds in fitting ground, and be pleased when those which he had sowed reached their perfection in the eighth month?”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates contrasts the serious farmer, who sows in properly suited ground and waits, with quick hothouse 'gardens of Adonis'.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates' serious farmer, like Valluvar's, trusts the proper preparation of the ground rather than shortcuts.
philosophy.source: Plato, Phaedrus 276b (tr. Harold N. Fowler, Loeb 1925, Perseus Digital Library)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Perseus; it shares the 'fitting ground' idea, but the passage is an analogy for teaching, not farming advice.

kurals.tamil:
ஏரினும் நன்றால் எருவிடுதல் கட்டபின்
நீரினும் நன்றதன் காப்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Erinum nandraal eruvidudhal kattapin
neerinum nandradhan kaappu.
kurals.meaning: Manuring is better than ploughing, and once the weeds are cleared, guarding the crop is better even than watering it.
kurals.elementary: Planting a garden is not the end of the job. You feed the soil, pull out the weeds, and then you have to protect the plants from birds, goats and trampling feet. Watching over what you grew matters even more than watering it.
kurals.university: The couplet ranks the farmer's tasks: eruviduthal (எருவிடுதல், 'applying manure') is better than Er (ஏர், 'ploughing'), and after katta (கட்ட, 'weeding'; Kesikan and Varadarasanar gloss kattapin as 'after removing weeds') kaappu (காப்பு, 'guarding, protection') is better than neer (நீர், 'watering'). Puliyur Kesikan, following Parimelazhagar, reads the sequence as plough, manure, weed, water, guard, with each later step more decisive than the one before it; Kalaignar's paraphrase ranks weeding and watering as 'very good' and protection as best. The point is that the work ends with vigilant protection of what has been produced, a principle the Porutpal applies to wealth as well as crops. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “May the Field's Lord for us be full of sweetness, and may we follow after him uninjured.”
hinduism.explanation: The Vedic farmers invoke Kshetrapati, the Lord or guardian of the Field, to keep the field and its workers safe and fruitful.
hinduism.tie_back: The hymn appeals to a guardian of the field, a religious form of the Kural's stress on protecting the crop.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 4.57.3 (tr. Ralph T.H. Griffith, 1896, sacred-texts.com)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the guardian-of-the-field idea is only loosely related to the Kural's practical advice to guard the crop.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The kingdom of heaven is likened unto a man which sowed good seed in his field: But while men slept, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat, and went his way.”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus' parable the field is spoiled because no one watched it while the workers slept.
christianity.tie_back: Unguarded fields are ruined, so watching over a crop matters as much as sowing it, as the Kural says.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it illustrates the danger of an unguarded field, though the parable is about the end of the age, not farm practice.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever keeps a dog, one Qirat of the reward of his good deeds is deducted daily, unless the dog is used for guarding a farm or cattle.”
islam.explanation: Islamic law makes a specific exception for dogs that guard crops and livestock, recognising the need to protect a farm.
islam.tie_back: Guarding the crop is important enough to override a general rule, which matches the Kural's high ranking of kaappu.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; it shows that guarding crops was legally valued, but does not rank guarding above other farm tasks.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Catch us the foxes, The little foxes That ruin the vineyards— For our vineyard is in blossom.”
judaism.explanation: The lovers' song calls for the vineyard to be protected from the small animals that damage it just when it blooms.
judaism.tie_back: Guarding the growing crop at its most vulnerable stage is the Kural's kaappu.
judaism.source: Song of Songs 2:15 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; it does picture crop protection, but in a love song usually read allegorically.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “whatsoever wealth a householder is in possession of, obtained by dint of effort, collected by strength of arm, by the sweat of his brow, justly acquired by right means — such he husbands well by guarding and watching so that kings would not seize it, thieves would not steal it, fire would not burn it, water would not carry it away”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names arakkha-sampada, the accomplishment of watchfulness, as essential for keeping what effort has produced.
buddhism.tie_back: Guarding what one's labour has produced is the Kural's kaappu, which it ranks above further inputs.
buddhism.source: Dighajanu (Vyagghapajja) Sutta, AN 8.54 (tr. Narada Thera, accesstoinsight.org)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong match on protecting what has been produced, though it speaks of wealth rather than crops.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If you do not give me what I ask for, I who observe the Samitis, who am protected by the Guptis, who subdue my senses, what benefit, then, will you gain by your sacrifices?”
jainism.explanation: The Jain monk is 'protected by the guptis', the three guards over mind, speech and body that keep new karma from flowing in.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain guptis apply the Kural's lesson inwardly: after cultivating virtue, one must guard it.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.17 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, sacred-texts.com)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the gupti concept of guarding is an analogy only, since Jain monks do not guard crops.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Let a slave follow a little behind with a mattock and make trouble for the birds by hiding the seed; for good management is the best for mortal men as bad management is the worst.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod advises posting a helper with a mattock behind the sower to keep the birds from the seed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod's guard behind the plough is the Kural's kaappu, which it values above more inputs.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 469-471 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White, 1914, sacred-texts.com)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong practical parallel on guarding seed and crop.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “If you want to make men fit to take charge, you must supervise their work and examine it, and be ready to reward work well carried through, and not shrink from punishing carelessness as it deserves.”
philosophy.explanation: Ischomachus insists that a farm prospers only under constant supervision and careful attention.
philosophy.tie_back: Constant watchfulness over the work, rather than more inputs, is what secures the yield, which is close to the Kural's ranking.
philosophy.source: Xenophon, Oeconomicus 12.19 (tr. E.C. Marchant, Loeb 1923, Perseus Digital Library)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Perseus; it is about supervising workers rather than guarding the crop, so it is only a partial match.

kurals.tamil:
செல்லான் கிழவன் இருப்பின் நிலம்புலந்து
இல்லாளின் ஊடி விடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Sellaan kizhavan iruppin nilampulandhu
illaaLin ooti vidum.
kurals.meaning: If the owner stays at home and does not go out to his land, the land will sulk and turn away from him like a neglected wife.
kurals.elementary: If you plant a garden and then forget about it, the plants droop and the weeds take over, as if the garden were upset with you. Valluvar says land is like a family member: it needs you to show up and care for it every day.
kurals.university: kizhavan (கிழவன்) here means 'owner' (of the land), not 'old man'; sellaan iruppin (செல்லான் இருப்பின்) means 'if he stays without going (to the field)'. The land then pulandhu (புலந்து, 'feeling aggrieved') and oodi vidum (ஊடி விடும், 'turns away in sulking') like an illaaL (இல்லாள், 'wife'). The verbs pulavi and oodal are technical terms of the Kamaththuppal for a lover's quarrel (compare chapters 131-133), so Valluvar borrows the vocabulary of love to describe neglected land. Puliyur Kesikan, following Parimelazhagar, glosses that the owner must go daily and do what is needed; Solomon Pappaiah spells out that the land, like a wife, first withers inwardly and then withholds its yield. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Auspicious Sītā, come thou near: we venerate and worship thee That thou mayst bless and prosper us and bring us fruits abundantly.”
hinduism.explanation: In the Vedic field hymn the furrow is personified as the goddess Sita, who must be approached and honoured before she bears fruit.
hinduism.tie_back: The Veda, like the Kural, treats the field as a feminine presence whose yield depends on the attention it receives.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 4.57.6 (tr. Ralph T.H. Griffith, 1896, sacred-texts.com)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it shares the image of the land as a woman to be attended to, but not the warning about the owner's neglect.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I went by the field of the slothful, and by the vineyard of the man void of understanding; And, lo, it was all grown over with thorns, and nettles had covered the face thereof, and the stone wall thereof was broken down.”
christianity.explanation: The wise man walks past the neglected field of a lazy owner and finds it overgrown and ruined.
christianity.tie_back: A field abandoned by its owner turns against him, which is the Kural's warning.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near match on the ruin of a field its owner neglects, without the wife simile.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever has land should cultivate it himself or give it to his (Muslim) brother gratis; otherwise keep it uncultivated.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet tells landholders to work their land themselves, or give it to someone who will, rather than profit from it at a distance.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, the hadith expects a landholder to attend to his own land in person.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; it encourages working one's own land, but its main context is renting land for a share of the crop, not neglect.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Mind well the looks of your flock; Pay attention to your herds; For property does not last forever, Or a crown for all generations.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs tells the owner to keep a personal eye on his livestock, since wealth that is neglected does not last.
judaism.tie_back: Proverbs, like the Kural, says an owner's personal attention is what keeps land and livestock productive.
judaism.source: Proverbs 27:23-24 (JPS Tanakh, Gender-Sensitive Edition 2023, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a strong match on the owner's personal attention, applied to flocks rather than fields.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is the case where a farming householder has three fields: one excellent field, one middling, and one poor—sandy, salty, with bad soil. … he would sow the seed first in the excellent field.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses a farmer who knows and attends to each of his fields as an image of a teacher who knows his listeners.
buddhism.tie_back: The farmer's close knowledge of his own fields reflects the owner's personal attention that the Kural requires.
buddhism.source: Desana Sutta, SN 42.7 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu, dhammatalks.org)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (ellipsis marks omitted words); it is about choosing fields rather than neglecting them, so this is a weak, next-best match.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Three merchants set out on their travels, each with his capital; one of them gained there much, the second returned with his capital, and the third merchant came home after having lost his capital. This parable is taken from common life; learn (to apply it) to the Law.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's parable warns that capital that is neglected is lost, and applies this to human life and spiritual gain.
jainism.tie_back: Neglected resources turn into loss, the warning the Kural gives the absent landowner.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.14-15 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, sacred-texts.com)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it shares the idea of neglect leading to loss, but concerns merchants and the soul, not land.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Do not put your work off till to-morrow and the day after; for a sluggish worker does not fill his barn, nor one who puts off his work”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns that a farmer who keeps postponing his field work will have an empty barn.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The farmer who stays away from his work loses the harvest, the Kural's land that withholds itself.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 410-412 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White, 1914, sacred-texts.com)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a solid match on neglect leading to a poor harvest, without the wife simile.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “So he asked one who was reputed clever with horses what is the quickest way of fattening a horse. ‘The master's eye,’ replied the man. I think we may apply the answer generally, Socrates, and say that the master's eye in the main does the good and worthy work.”
philosophy.explanation: Ischomachus cites the Persian proverb that the owner's own eye is what makes his property thrive.
philosophy.tie_back: 'The master's eye' is almost exactly the Kural's demand that the owner go to his land himself.
philosophy.source: Xenophon, Oeconomicus 12.20 (tr. E.C. Marchant, Loeb 1923, Perseus Digital Library)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Perseus (nested quotation marks normalised); a near one-to-one parallel on the owner's personal attention.

kurals.tamil:
இலமென்று அசைஇ இருப்பாரைக் காணின்
நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள் நகும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ilamendru asaii iruppaaraik kaaNin
nilamennum nallaaL nakum.
kurals.meaning: When the good lady called Earth sees people sitting idle and saying 'we have nothing', she laughs to herself.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone sitting beside a big empty field and complaining, 'I have nothing to eat!' Valluvar says the Earth would giggle, because the field is right there, ready to grow food for anyone willing to work it.
kurals.university: ilam endru (இலம் என்று, 'saying "we have nothing"') and asaii iruppaar (அசைஇ இருப்பார், 'those who sit idle', with asaii lengthened by alapedai) are the people the Earth laughs at. nilam ennum nallaaL (நிலம் என்னும் நல்லாள்) means 'the good woman called Earth', and nakum (நகும்) means 'will laugh'. Puliyur Kesikan, following Parimelazhagar, says she laughs to herself, because the remedy for their poverty lies in her and needs only effort; Solomon Pappaiah reads the laughter as mockery, and Kalaignar names her Bhoomiththaai (Mother Earth). The chapter ends where it began, with land as the answer to want, and leads directly into Nalkuravu (ch. 105, Poverty). Pope's rendering is 'The earth, that kindly dame, will laugh to see, / Men seated idle pleading poverty.' The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Perform your prescribed duty, for doing so is better than not working. One cannot even maintain one’s physical body without work.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that action is better than inaction and that even keeping the body alive requires work.
hinduism.tie_back: Sitting idle and pleading want contradicts the plain fact the Gita states and the Kural's Earth laughs at.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.8 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda, vedabase.io)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; strong on work over idleness, though the Gita speaks of prescribed duty in general, not farming.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The sluggard will not plow by reason of the cold; therefore shall he beg in harvest, and have nothing.”
christianity.explanation: The lazy man who will not plough in season ends up begging at harvest time.
christianity.tie_back: The sluggard's self-made poverty is exactly what the Kural's Earth laughs at.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match on idleness, ploughing and self-caused poverty.

islam.quote_or_event: “It is He who made the earth tame for you - so walk among its slopes and eat of His provision - and to Him is the resurrection.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents the earth as made ready for human use and tells people to go out into it and seek their provision.
islam.tie_back: The earth is ready and waiting, so idling and pleading poverty is what the Kural's Earth laughs at.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud; it implies an earth ready to provide for those who exert themselves, but does not rebuke idleness directly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rava said to the Sages who would attend his study hall: I implore you; during the months of Nisan and Tishrei, the crucial agricultural periods, do not appear before me. Engage in your agricultural work then so that you will not be preoccupied with your sustenance all year.”
judaism.explanation: Even the great teacher Rava sends his students to their fields in the farming seasons rather than have them neglect their livelihood.
judaism.tie_back: Rava expects even scholars to farm in season rather than plead want, in keeping with the Kural.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 35b (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria (bold-face markup removed; the bracketed gloss 'the crucial agricultural periods' is Steinsaltz's); a reasonable match on working the land rather than idling, without the mocking Earth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The idler who does not exert himself when he should, who though young and strong is full of sloth, with a mind full of vain thoughts — such an indolent man does not find the path to wisdom.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada condemns the able-bodied person who sits in sloth when he should be making an effort.
buddhism.tie_back: The strong idler is the person the Kural's Earth laughs at, though here the loss is spiritual rather than economic.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong match on idleness by those able to act, but the goal is wisdom, not a harvest.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fallow leaf of the tree falls to the ground, when its days are gone, even so the life of men (will come to its close); Gautama, be careful all the while!”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira repeatedly urges his disciple never to be careless (pramada) for even a moment, because life is short.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain refrain against negligence matches the Kural's scorn for idle people who let what is in reach go unused.
jainism.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 10.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, sacred-texts.com)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it shares the theme of rejecting negligence, but is aimed at a monk's spiritual vigilance, not at livelihood or farming.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Work is no disgrace: it is idleness which is a disgrace. But if you work, the idle will soon envy you as you grow rich”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells Perses that idleness, not labour, is shameful, and that the worker soon prospers.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod's scorn for the idle matches the Earth's laughter at those who sit and plead poverty.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 311-313 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White, 1914, sacred-texts.com)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near match on the shame of idleness in a farming setting.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Of course there are—sluggards must be included; for you can't do your own business when you are asleep, nor make others do theirs.”
philosophy.explanation: Ischomachus names sluggards, alongside drunkards, as people who can never become careful managers of a farm.
philosophy.tie_back: The sleeping sluggard who gets nothing done is the idle person the Kural's Earth laughs at.
philosophy.source: Xenophon, Oeconomicus 12.12 (tr. E.C. Marchant, Loeb 1923, Perseus Digital Library)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Perseus; it shares the theme of sloth in farm management but not the image of poverty-pleading or laughter.
